posts.author: Guillermito
posts.content_md:
Zebra Imaging did this many years ago. I saw one of the early result from close in the Benton MIT lab where they started. Then Geola and/or XYZ (there are some videos on Geola site). Full-color printed holography based on small pixels. I actually do believe that this technique is the future of display holography, if someone manages to reduce the price. I mean, this can actually have many commercial / marketing usages, unlike good old monochromatic film-based holography (which I dearly love, but I think it's just an evolutionary dead end, commercialy speaking). And you don't have to create an actual scene, everything is made with 3D-software.

Geola tried to sell their enormous "Space Station" hologram on eBay a few month ago, if I remember correctly. I don't remember the price, but it was way too high, just like these ones from XYZ. Nobody made a bid. I suggested to them that they should try with smaller ones.

Indeed, Geola and XYZ work together. From the "history" part of their website :

"In 2001 Geola UAB became a major shareholder of the Canadian company XYZ Imaging Inc which had offered to raise the finance required to take Geola’s prototype 1-step printing technology and develop it into a real commercial printer.

By early 2002 Geola had delivered a working RGB prototype dot-matrix printer to Montreal. This printer (see above) was able to generate full-colour reflection holograms by printing 15 RGB holopixels each second onto glass holoplates."

posts.author: holokid
posts.content_md:
It's a small holographic world isn't it… XYZ Imaging, Geola, Zebra, Liti etc. etc 

Just to clarify a couple issues though...

Geola uses the XYZ Imaging printer to produce the color holo's seen on various Geola related sites. They were once shareholder of Imaging but not any more. The recent systems developed by Imaging use proprietary lasers developed by Imaging, which is especially true for very large holo’s where laser stabilization is a key factor.

Zebra's holo's are typically created with CW lasers on glass (4 sq. ft max) using a dry film technology, very long process and typically more expensive. Imaging's are single write on film which is a wide format 1.2 meters by the length of the role, compareatively fast and cheaper. Zebra prints full parallax where the image is rendered on the fly (lower quality CG models required), where-as Imaging uses pre-rendered Hollywood imagery to achieve superior quality in single parallax fashion. While Imaging’s printers can print full parallax the memory requirements would be insane i.e. 1024x2048 high-definition fully CG scenes> if one frame only took a minute to render then a full parallax scene would take 4 years to render completely. 

Question: What do people think the market will bare for full color holo art and what is a good size, is bigger not better ?

posts.author: Stas
posts.content_md:
[quote="holokid"]It's a small holographic world isn't it… XYZ Imaging, Geola, Zebra, Liti etc. etc 

Just to clarify things more:

The digital holography with pulsed laser was developed by Geola, patent priority from december 1999. The RGB pulsed laser for holography also was developed by Geola in 2000. Then various laser energy stabilisation schemes were developed by Geola and by XYZ. At the moment here in Vilnius (Geola EU office) we have one printer which working principles are based on Geola first patent. The printer was manufactured by XYZ. 

The diffference between our holograms and those of XYZ and Zebra is that we mostly are printing the life scenes, like museum artefacts, portraits etc. For that we have built the "camera-on-a-rail" type device that shoots and prepares the files suitable for the printer.

To those who like to read scientific articles I've put our three latest ones for download on [http://www.geola.lt/download/Geola_arti ... 06_pdf.zip](http://www.geola.lt/download/Geola_articles_2006_pdf.zip)

posts.author: Stas
posts.content_md:
I personally like more the article on our latest kid - HoloShot. I think this device is quite important for the holography - it separates the hologram origination process from the hologram printing (while using the digital printers). And can be operated by any photographer or filmmaker apprentice.

That drags the holography back to the mainstream of advertising and special products presentations businesses. I've already faced situations when the digital holograms were rejected by the adds agencies only because all their photographers and other imaging guys were not involved in the image origination. And those agencies quite rarely have a good 3d designer that can prepare the scene for digital printers properly.

But now everybody in the adds production chain can be happy by participating in holograms magic creation.
